entry.evidence: However, the mechanisms and boundary conditions allowing the coeval existence of different tectonic regimes are not yet fully understood.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) with PDF for figures

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the ratio of stretching to shortening rates, crustal strength and inheritance (including basin reactivation) control coeval tectonic regimes, noting the lack of systematic study.
steps.quote: there is a lack of systematic investigation of the role of the relative ratio between shortening and stretching rates

steps.action: They build the apparatus: a sand layer (strong crust) or sand over PDMS (weak crust) on a compressible foam base driven by step-motor pistons, with material properties taken from published benchmarks.
steps.quote: To simulate the ductile part of the crust, we use PDMS silicone

steps.action: They check that the apparatus is dynamically similar to the crust by computing stress, strain-rate, time and velocity ratios and comparing Ramberg and Rs numbers between model and nature.
steps.quote: The dynamic similarity between our experiments and the natural case for the viscous regime is verified by computing the ratio

steps.action: They design one-stage and two-stage runs with a central silicone seed and a grid of Ve/Vs boundary conditions (Fig. 3), with no surface processes, to study reactivation or inversion of first-stage structures.
steps.quote: two-stage experiments with a first phase of 5 % stretching and a second phase with either shortening only or synchronous orthogonal shortening and stretching

steps.action: They set up the analysis chain: top-view photographs every 2 min, CLAHE filtering, PIVlab velocity fields at about 4 mm resolution, and StrainMap Hencky-strain classification of fault type.
steps.quote: It allows us to discriminate between coexisting strike-slip faults, thrust faults, and normal faults

steps.action: They run five single-stage brittle models with Ve/Vs from 0 to 2.8 (BI10, BI09, BI05, BI06, BI07).
steps.quote: we performed a series of five single-stage models in which the ratio of stretching velocity over shortening velocity V e / V s is varied

steps.action: They observe in-sequence thrusts at low Ve/Vs, edge normal faults for Ve>0, and a central graben with conjugate strike-slip faults at higher Ve/Vs.
steps.quote: deformation is partitioned between shortening that is accommodated along an E–W thrust fault, diffuse extension in the retrowedge, and strike-slip faults

steps.action: They run two-stage brittle models (BI01, BI08, BI11) with an initial E–W extension before second-stage shortening at Ve/Vs = 0, 1.4 and 2.
steps.quote: they undergo an initial stage of E–W extension with up to 5 %–5.3 % of stretching prior to a second stage of N–S shortening

steps.action: They compare each two-stage model with its single-stage counterpart (BI01 vs BI10, BI08 vs BI05, BI11 vs BI06): thrusts branch, localization is earlier, and strike-slip orientations differ.
steps.quote: The pattern of deformation after 4 % of shortening differs from model BI05 with similar boundary conditions but no initial stage of stretching

steps.action: They run the brittle–ductile single-stage model CE16 at Ve/Vs = 0.9 to test the effect of crustal strength.
steps.quote: The model CE16 has been performed to test how the deformation distribution evolves as a function of the strength of the crust

steps.action: They compare CE16 with brittle BI09 under the same Ve/Vs: diffuse shortening and corner strike-slip faults, a back-thrust, and no normal faults.
steps.quote: Unlike model BI09, there are no N–S normal faults at this stage.

steps.action: They run the two-stage brittle–ductile model CE17 with 4.7 % initial E–W stretching before coeval shortening and stretching.
steps.quote: The model CE17 is similar to model CE16 except that we impose an initial stage of 4.7 % E–W stretching.

steps.action: They compare CE17 with CE16 and with brittle BI08: inherited normal faults reactivate as normal or shortening-parallel strike-slip faults, and no E–W thrust forms.
steps.quote: the brittle-only model exhibits a clear E–W thrust fault that is not observed in the brittle–ductile model

steps.action: They run and describe CE18 (Ve/Vs = 0.7) and CE20 (Ve/Vs = 1.1): diffuse shortening with limited normal reactivation in CE18, and broad normal reactivation in CE20.
steps.quote: large portions of the pre-existing western, eastern, and central normal faults are reactivated as normal faults during the second stage of deformation

steps.action: They compare plane-strain runs with the Andersonian expectation of transport-orthogonal normal or thrust faults and find agreement; non-plane-strain runs combine all three fault types.
steps.quote: Our models confirm that under plane-strain conditions

steps.action: They infer principal-stress orientations and regime permutations in zones of BI05 with a Mohr–Coulomb analysis, including wedge loading that drives thrust propagation.
steps.quote: The Mohr–Coulomb analysis for a frictional material like sand also implies that the differential stress necessary for material failure is maximal for thrust faults

steps.action: They state the Ve/Vs ranges for coexistence of the three regimes in brittle models and their absence in brittle–ductile models, with the caveat that the imposed shortening is limited.
steps.quote: the coexistence of the three types of structures (after 10 % of E–W stretching) starts for V e / V s ratios > 1.4

steps.action: They compare fault orientations with the Coulomb criterion: most fit, but northern strike-slip faults lie at 60–70° to σ1.
steps.quote: a majority of the structures are consistent with the Coulomb fracture criterion

steps.action: They propose rival explanations for the anomalous strike-slip orientations: wall boundary effects, rotation of σ1, or control by the central graben.
steps.quote: we cannot exclude that they result from some unwanted boundary effects associated with the high friction wall–sand interface

steps.action: They use BI05 as a reference for BI08 (same Ve/Vs, no initial stretching) and find no anomalous southern strike-slip faults in BI05, which supports control by pre-existing structures.
steps.quote: model BI05, which shares the same stretching / shortening ratio and almost the same amount of total stretching

steps.action: They keep the regularity that normal and thrust faults keep fixed orientations, while strike-slip orientations range from about 0° to 65° depending on strength and inheritance.
steps.quote: both normal faults and thrust faults remain with similar orientations, i.e., N–S and E–W, respectively

steps.action: They compare models of different strength (BI09 vs CE16) and with or without initial stretching (CE17 vs CE16), and explain the differences by brittle-layer thickness and local thinning.
steps.quote: This can readily be explained by the decrease by a factor of 2 of the thickness of the brittle crust in the weak models.

steps.action: They conclude that inheritance and strength control the structures, so fault associations do not indicate Ve/Vs unless the deformation history is known (synthesis in Fig. 11).
steps.quote: the association of specific types of faults cannot be used as an indicator of the relative rate of shortening and stretching

steps.action: Motivated by the San Jorge basin, they pose the question of how extensional structures reactivate under fault-parallel contraction.
steps.quote: We therefore more specifically explored the conditions leading to the reactivation of extensional structures under fault-parallel contraction

steps.action: They keep the result that inherited normal faults are never inverted, are not reactivated without orthogonal stretching (BI01), and reactivate as strike-slip or normal faults as Ve/Vs increases.
steps.quote: there is no clear evidence that normal faults lying parallel to the contraction direction are inverted as contractional structures

steps.action: They compare their results with earlier analog and numerical models (Dhifaoui, Corti, Duarte/Rosas, Le Pourhiet, Cruden) and with natural V-shaped conjugate systems in Anatolia, the Alps, Tibet and Central Asia.
steps.quote: The absence of strike-slip faults is therefore consistent with our minimum value

steps.action: To explain why their basins are not inverted, unlike earlier inversion models, they propose coeval orthogonal extension as the cause.
steps.quote: This difference could result from the boundary conditions applied in our models BI08-11 and CE17–20

steps.action: They use BI01 (no stretching during shortening, still no inversion) to reject boundary conditions as the sole control and invoke internal parameters (weak-zone size, crustal thinning, surface processes, isostasy).
steps.quote: this may not be the only controlling factor given that in model BI01, which does not have stretching applied during shortening

steps.action: They compare two-stage reactivation patterns with synorogenic foreland transtensional reactivation in the Baikal rift and the San Jorge Gulf basin.
steps.quote: our models are compatible with natural cases of synorogenic foreland rifting–transtensional reactivations

steps.action: They keep the Ve/Vs thresholds for two and three coexisting regimes as a possible minimum for lateral escape, and keep weak crust as favoring conjugate strike-slip systems.
steps.quote: the three regimes operate simultaneously when V e / V s is ≥ 1.4 , possibly indicating a minimum value in this ratio for effective [...]

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of preprint egusphere-2022-62 (RC1, AC1, RC2, AC2, EC1); AC1/AC2 supplements are font-encoded, so quotes are taken from readable comments only

steps.action: Referee 2 questions imposing lateral extrusion by boundary conditions; the authors add the rationale (precise control of Ve/Vs; far-field forces producing orthogonal stretching) to the Introduction and Procedure.
steps.quote: I think that some more discussion on the rationale of the modelling and its comparison with previous models would be necessary

steps.action: Referee 2 objects to the terms indentation and extrusion rates; the authors replace them with shortening and stretching rates throughout, including the title.
steps.quote: So why not use the terms shortening rate and extension rate? Please comment on this.

steps.action: In answer to referee questions on the low PDMS density, sand cohesion and dimensionless numbers, the authors explain the PDMS choice (engine speeds), run unpublished 2D numerical tests of density, add cohesion references, and add Rm and Rs to Table 2.
steps.quote: Please clarify the choice of the PDMS silicone (technical advantages?).

steps.action: Asked about side-wall friction causing thrust convexity, the authors reply that no friction-reducing practice was used and that the convexity lies in the model centre; no new work is done.
steps.quote: Have you adopted any technical practices to minimize this effect?

steps.action: Both referees ask for more comparison with prior models; the authors add Duarte, Rosas, Krstekanić, Philippon, van Gelder, Corti and Le Pourhiet to the Introduction and Discussion.
steps.page: RC2 ¶9; RC1 ¶3; AC1-S p.1; AC2-S p.4
steps.quote: Corti et al. (2006, Spec. Paper GSA) performed similar analogue models characterised by coeval shortening and orthogonal extension

steps.action: Referee 1 asks that section 4.1 address accumulated strain and wedge loading; the authors add the limited-shortening caveat for high-Ve/Vs brittle models and the wedge-thickening effect on vertical stress.
Both referees ask whether the anomalous strike-slip faults are boundary effects; the authors add boundary effects and σ1 rotation as rival explanations while keeping graben control.
steps.quote: Have you considered the possibility that these anomalous faults departing from the edges of the graben could represent only boundary effects?

steps.action: Referee 2 questions the expected shortening-parallel thrusting in BI01; the authors rewrite the paragraph and add Sokoutis et al. (2000) on isostasy and thickness contrasts.
steps.quote: Spontaneous shortening-parallel thrusting resulted in the above-mentioned model by Sokoutis et al (2000)

steps.action: Referee 2 asks about the kinematics of reactivated normal faults; the authors state that natural basins were reactivated in transtension.
steps.quote: What is the dominant kinematics of reactivated normal faults?

steps.action: The editor asks the authors to consider Cruden et al. (2006) and Rosenberg et al. (2007); both are incorporated in the Discussion (§4.5 ¶3).
steps.quote: Though both studies are done on the scale of the lithosphere, the results are important for understanding lateral transitions

tree.answer: Coeval thrust, normal and strike-slip regimes documented in nature (Fig. 1).
No; controlling boundary conditions are not observable in nature, so scaled analog models with PIV strain imaging are used.
Map how Ve/Vs, crustal strength and inheritance control fault types, locations and reactivation.
No rivals at the outset; rivals appear only for anomalous strike-slip orientations and for the lack of inversion.
Conditions set in the laboratory (piston velocities, layering, seeds, two-stage history).
Partly: scaling check and single-stage reference models; one run per condition, no repeats.
Regime map over Ve/Vs, strength and inheritance kept, with stated limits on the amount of shortening.
Yes; minor/moderate revision with added literature, rationale and caveats.

end.claim: In brittle models the three fault regimes coexist at intermediate-to-high Ve/Vs (≥ ~1.4), but never in brittle–ductile models; inherited normal faults are never inverted under fault-parallel shortening and instead reactivate as strike-slip or normal faults as Ve/Vs increases.

decisive_move.sentence: The systematic laboratory runs setting Ve/Vs, crustal layering and a prior extensional stage (12 models, Fig. 3) produce the regime map on which every claim rests.

gates.evidence: Runs were designed as a parameter sweep under an open question (§1 ¶2–¶3), not to test a stated hypothesis. Results were compared with Andersonian plane-strain and Coulomb expectations (§4.1 ¶1, §4.2 ¶1), which they could have failed, but the headline thresholds were read off the runs after the fact. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Particle image velocimetry (PIVlab) for surface velocity fields
CLAHE contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization filter
Hencky (logarithmic) strain description of shape change (StrainMap)
PDMS silicone and polyurethane foam RG35 as analog materials

novelty_claims.quote: We also analyze the role of crustal inheritance in fault reactivation and potential basin inversion during coeval shortening and lateral extension, which has not been [...]
allow us to gain new insights into geological areas recording the simultaneous activity of different deformation regimes

limits: Composition none_fits: this is a laboratory parameter sweep posed under an open question, with no rivals until the Discussion; it is closest to exploration_first, but a question precedes the variation. Each boundary condition was run once; there are no repeat runs, so reproducibility is not shown. The Ve/Vs threshold for three coexisting regimes is stated inconsistently: 1.4 < Ve/Vs < 2 in §0 ¶1, > 1.4 in §4.1 ¶3, ≥ 1.4 in §4.5 ¶1 and §5 ¶4, and > 1 in §5 ¶2. The minimum for lateral escape is given as > 0.9 (§4.5 ¶2) and ≥ 0.9 (§5 ¶4). The authors note that the limited amount of shortening may hide later thrusting (§4.1 ¶3–¶4); the regularity therefore holds only within ≤ ~14 % shortening. Sub-claims and their statuses: the control of anomalous strike-slip orientations by graben or inheritance is best_explanation, with boundary effects not excluded (§4.2 ¶1–¶2). The internal-parameter explanation of non-inversion is best_explanation (§4.5 ¶5). The analogy to natural cases (Anatolia, Alps, Tibet, Central Asia, Baikal, San Jorge) is qualitative resemblance without a test. The density-effect 2D numerical test appears only in the author response (AC2-S p.3, inferred from decoded text) and not in the published paper. RC1's specific comments were in an annotated PDF that was not supplied; RC1's requests are inferred from the font-encoded AC1 replies, so the review steps citing AC1-S carry empty quotes. Figure-layout changes requested by RC1 and RC2 (panel letters, supplementary stretch plots, seed labels) are not coded as steps.

disagreements.target: Previous basin inversion analog models (Del Ventisette et al. 2006; Sani et al. 2007; Deng et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: Their two-stage models with basin-parallel shortening show no inversion, attributed partly to coeval orthogonal extension and partly to internal parameters, with BI01 as evidence.
disagreements.quote: These results differ from previous basin inversion analog models

disagreements.target: Brittle thrust–wrench interference analog models (Duarte et al. 2011; Rosas et al. 2012, 2015)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that confined walls and prescribed fault directions in those setups prevented V-shaped strike-slip systems from developing.
disagreements.quote: strike-slip fault strike and activity were constrained by the chosen setup that included confined walls

disagreements.target: Inversion modeling studies applying parallel or low-angle stretching and contraction (McClay 1995; Bonini et al. 2012; Zwaan et al. 2022)
disagreements.support: The San Jorge basin shows contraction parallel to normal faults, a configuration the earlier setups did not cover and these experiments explore.
disagreements.quote: In general, the applied directions of stretching and successive contraction are parallel

alternatives_considered.chosen: Low-density PDMS (965 kg m-3) as the ductile layer
alternatives_considered.reason: Increasing density would raise viscosity and require piston speeds too low for the engines; buoyancy effects considered limited by high viscosity and short duration

alternatives_considered.chosen: No surface processes (grabens left unfilled between stages)
alternatives_considered.reason: To ensure similar conditions between models, hard to achieve with manual intervention

alternatives_considered.chosen: Natural crustal viscosity of 10^21 Pa s for scaling
alternatives_considered.reason: Within the range of proposed values

alternatives_considered.chosen: StrainMap Hencky-strain classification of fault type
Graben or inherited-structure control on anomalous strike-slip orientation, with other factors possibly combined
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Wall–sand boundary effects; rotation of σ1
alternatives_considered.reason: Variable orientations within a model and the BI05 vs BI08 contrast

alternatives_considered.chosen: Internal parameters (weak-zone size, crustal thinning, surface processes, isostasy) together with boundary conditions
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Coeval orthogonal extension alone as the cause of non-inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: BI01, without stretching during shortening, also shows no inversion
